counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem titled “A Cavalcade of Waynes,” packed with puns, pop-culture references, working-class British imagery, and many different men named Wayne, ending with them forming an arch for the speaker to walk through like both bridegroom and bride.
counterfactuals.output:
# A Cavalcade of Waynes

At chucking-out time the Waynes came down our street in a cavalcade of white vans, mobility scooters and one knackered Cortina whose exhaust sang *Bohemian Rhapsody* through a sock. First came Wayne Rooney, nutmegging a turnip between the wheelie bins; then Wayne Sleep, pirouetting past the off-licence in steel-toe-capped boots. Wayne Bridge bridged the gutter with two planks nicked from a skip, while Wayne Routledge took the long way round, via Huddersfield, three bus replacements and a Greggs.

“Party time, excellent,” cried Wayne Campbell from the passenger seat of reality, headbanging to the rattle of loose change. Behind him, Bruce Wayne had parked the Batmobile on double yellows outside the working men’s club, where John Wayne—Wayne by surname, cowboy by municipal decree—ordered a pint of mild and called the barmaid pilgrim. She told him to sling his hook.

The sky began to Wayne. Not rain: Wayne. Little men in hi-vis fell softly onto the allotments, each carrying a flask, a folded racing page and an opinion about the council. Wayne Hemingway redesigned the launderette in seaside colours. Wayne Fontana repaired the jukebox with a butter knife. Wayne Hussey announced a mission, though nobody knew whether it was Gothic, Mormon or just to fetch chips. Wayne McGregor choreographed the queue at the cashpoint: step, sigh, check balance, recoil.

Every Wayne had a trade. Wayne the Drain unblocked the moon. Wayne the Crane lifted Tuesday clear over the rooftops. Wayne the Pain worked collections for British Gas. Wayne the Main stood under the flyover shouting that he was the principal Wayne, the A-road Wayne, the one true carriage-Wayne, until Wayne the Lesser lamped him with a rolled-up *Mirror*. There was a weigh-in of Waynes by the fruit machine, but all were found wanting, or at least wanting another round.

Their mothers called from upstairs windows: *Wayne! Your tea’s going cold!* A hundred heads turned. A hundred tattooed forearms rose in apology. Somewhere a pressure cooker hissed; somewhere a baby wore a tiny Manchester United kit; somewhere a bloke named Dwayne insisted the D was silent and was admitted to the brotherhood after a show of hands.

By midnight they filled the precinct: Wayne Knights and Wayne manors, Waynes waxing and Waynes waning, Waynes of all works and masters of none. They smelled of Swarfega, Lynx Africa, wet denim, chip fat and the noble grief of Sunday-night telly. They sang “Wonderwall” one word behind the guitar. They carried me shoulder-high past the shuttered pawnbroker’s, past the kebab shop’s revolving galaxy, past the bus shelter where our names had been scratched into Perspex by keys that opened nothing.

Then, without foreman or whistle, the Waynes arranged themselves in two long rows. Wayne Bridge clasped hands with Bruce Wayne; Rooney with Sleep; Campbell with John; every Wayne found his opposite, his double, his long-lost pun. Their arms rose over the pavement, making a vault beneath the sodium lamps—a nave of knuckles, watches and faded blue sleeves.

And I walked through their arch while they cheered and wept and called me mate, walking beneath all that Wayne-scotting, Wayne-wrighting glory, as solemn as a bridegroom and as radiant as a bride.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an experimental British poem in the style of Geoff Hattersley about dozens of Waynes in a pub, using crude humour, surreal nicknames, celebrity parodies, and repeated phrases. Finish with all the Waynes linking hands in two rows as the narrator marches beneath them.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t imitate Geoff Hattersley’s exact style, but here’s an original poem with blunt British pub surrealism, crude humour, obsessive repetition, celebrity spoofs, and a rowdy spoken-word pulse.

### WAYNE O’CLOCK

In the Dog & Stapler  
it was Wayne o’clock.

Wayne o’clock, landlord.  
Wayne o’clock, love.

There was Big Wayne,  
Little Wayne,  
Wayne the Human Ashtray,  
Wayne “Two Gravies” Sproston,  
Wayne with the haunted fleece,  
and Wayne whose arse had been barred  
before the rest of him.

At the fruit machine  
Sir David Attenborrow  
whispered—

*Here we see the lesser-spotted Wayne  
feeding naturally  
on dry-roasted peanuts  
and somebody else’s lager.*

Wayne said,  
Who’s that old git?

Wayne said,  
No idea, Wayne.

Wayne said,  
Wayne o’clock.

By the bog door stood  
Wayne Rooney’s Loony Cousin,  
Wayne Sleep Deprivation,  
Wayne Newton’s Cradle,  
and Wayne Gok Wan Kenobi  
in a silver anorak  
telling everybody:

May the sauce be with you.

The jukebox coughed up  
Queen.

Not Queen Queen.  
A Queen tribute band  
called Mild Royalty.

Freddie Mercury Poisoning  
wore a yellow marigold glove  
and sang:

I want to break wind,  
I want to break wind—

and thirty-seven Waynes  
raised thirty-seven pints  
to the patron saint  
of trapped air.

Wayne o’clock, landlord.  
Wayne o’clock, love.

Behind the bar,  
Adele Dazeem from Cash & Carry  
was crying into the optics.

Brad Pitt Pony  
had eaten the beer mat.

Johnny Debt  
owed everyone twenty quid.

Taylor Swift Half  
had been poured  
into a vase.

And Nigel Farage Against the Machine  
was shouting about sovereignty  
at a pickled egg.

The pickled egg  
won.

Then Wayne “Bus Replacement Service” Wayne  
arrived three hours late  
with no explanation.

Then Wayne the Weather  
rained indoors.

Then Wayne the Unlicensed Dentist  
took out his own tooth  
with the darts trophy  
and charged himself forty pounds.

Cash only, he said.

Cash only, Wayne.

Wayne o’clock.

In the toilets  
someone had written:

WAYNE LOVES—

then run out of wall.

Outside, the moon  
looked like a scotch egg  
God had bitten  
and quietly put back.

Inside, the carpet  
remembered every shoe,  
every fight,  
every dropped kebab,  
every heroic little puddle  
nobody admitted to.

Last orders.

Last orders, Wayne.

The Waynes became solemn.

Big Wayne took Little Wayne’s hand.  
Little Wayne took Wayne the Human Ashtray’s.  
Two Gravies took Haunted Fleece.  
Gok Wan Kenobi took Johnny Debt.  
Bus Replacement Service took the Weather.  
The barred arse took the rest of its Wayne.

They made two rows  
from the fruit machine  
to the door—

two long rows of Waynes  
linking hands overhead,  
a fleshy railway bridge,  
a cathedral of knuckles,  
a tunnel built from lager  
and terrible decisions.

Wayne o’clock, they chanted.

Wayne o’clock.

And I marched beneath them,  
upright as a fool in a borrowed hat,  
while all the Waynes linked hands  
and roared my name  
though none of them knew it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense comic monologue built around variations on the name “Wayne,” including references to Kanye West, Wayne’s World, “Sleng Teng,” “It’s Raining Men,” Fleabag, Fred Perry, Stacey, and “Away in a Manger.” Make the final sentence lyrical and triumphant.
counterfactuals.output:
My name is Wayne, which means every introduction becomes a traffic report: “Wayne’s here,” “Wayne’s delayed,” “Wayne will continue through the evening, occasionally heavy.” Kanye West sounds like a compass having a breakdown—“Can ye west?”—whereas I’m more practical: Wayne east, Wayne left at the lights, Wayne until you see a Fred Perry polo vibrating outside a pub. People shout “Wayne’s World!” at me, and I’m obliged to answer, “Party time, excellent,” even at funerals, tax audits, and one particularly tense episode of *Fleabag*. The priest looked straight at me, and I thought, Don’t flirt with him, Wayne; this is exactly how prestige television happens.

My mate Stacey says Wayne is not a name but a noise a sad horse makes. Stacey has no room to talk: her name sounds like a regional estate agent who calls every cupboard a “bonus bedroom.” She once dated Kanye West—or, technically, a man named Ken who lived west of Swindon—but she still describes the relationship as “my celebrity era.” They broke up over music. Ken wanted “Sleng Teng”; Stacey thought it was a Scandinavian trouser press. I tried explaining that it’s a foundational riddim, but she said, “Wayne, you pronounce *rhythm* like you’re carrying a wardrobe downstairs.”

Music follows me. At karaoke I requested “It’s Raining Men,” and the DJ announced, “It’s Wayne-ing Men,” which sounds less like a disco anthem and more like a council warning about blokes falling from a multistorey car park. Suddenly the room was full of Fred Perry collars, all turned up like tiny satellite dishes searching for lager. One man yelled “Schwing!” Another yelled “No way!” I yelled “Way,” because that is what remains when you remove the unnecessary consonants from destiny.

Even Christmas isn’t safe. Everyone else sings “Away in a Manger”; my family sings “A Wayne in a Manger,” and there I am beside the crib, forty-two years old, knees up around my ears, asking whether the wise men validate parking. No crib for a bed? Luxury. I once rented in London; my bed was a persuasive shelf. The landlord called it “Fleabag-adjacent,” meaning there was a fox outside and emotional damage included.

But I’ve accepted it: I am Wayne, not Kanye, not Bruce, not Rooney, not a catchphrase trapped in *Wayne’s World*, but a whole weather system in a Fred Perry crown—so let the Sleng Teng thunder, let the men rain down, let Stacey ring the bells, for away from the manger and into the morning I ride, laughing, blazing, and gloriously Wayne.
